document_title: Who Sets the Clock on a Plate Read
post_copy:
In the Anchorage mayor's version of the surveillance ordinance, a plate data "limit" is a reason, not a number.

The city's plate reader policy must limit storage "based on articulable operational needs." The sponsors' S-1 text names no number either.

Flock says it began installing plate readers for a private customer the week before October 5th. A crowdsourced map showed eight at two Anchorage Lowe's stores.

In the August 18th original, "limit" means 14 days and then deletion.

APD says it has no access to plate readers at privately owned locations.

Whatever "limit" means after October 20th, it will govern city readers, not store readers.

The three texts' clocks, the September definition built on AI, APD's 14-day policy and the store readers none reach.

Should Anchorage's plate data rules ever reach a reader on private property?

#AnchorageAssembly #PlateReaders #PrivacyLaw

slides.headline: 14 days in code, or a limit set in policy?
labels: ONE LOT, ONE STRIP A NIGHT

slides.headline: Three texts. One sets a day.
slides.body: The sponsors' August 18th original would delete plate data within 14 days, and searching older data would need a warrant. The mayor's September 15th substitute asks for a policy limit "based on articulable operational needs." The sponsors' own S-1 builds on the mayor's text.
labels: "permanently deleted no later than fourteen days after capture"

slides.headline: The original timed the live feed too.
slides.body: Live camera access would shut off after sixty minutes, renewed thirty at a time. Trials of new tools, 90 days at most. Plate reader authority, ending January 1st, 2031. The September texts set other clocks, 30 days to report a policy change and 45 to act on a complaint.
labels: ONE HOUR OF SKY · SIXTY MINUTES
SEPTEMBER TEXTS · TESTS AND PILOTS, NO STATED LIMIT

slides.headline: September's texts name artificial intelligence.
slides.body: Both define surveillance technology as tools that work "by using fully or partially-automated machine learning, artificial intelligence, or similar technology." The August original defined it by what a system collects.
labels: ILLUSTRATION · DASHCAM APD'S ONLY PLATE READERS, PER THE CHIEF IN AUGUST

slides.headline: There is already a 14.
slides.body: APD's own page says scanned plate data is deleted after 14 days. That's police policy on a web page, not code.

slides.kicker: SAVE THIS · AO 2026-108 SIDE BY SIDE
slides.headline: Three texts, side by side.
labels: LOWE'S STATEMENT, PER ADN · TYPICALLY NO MORE THAN 90 DAYS
GOLD PAINT · A NUMBER IN THE TEXT
WHITE PAINT · A POLICY OR NONE

slides.kicker: UNTIL RECENTLY, NO FLOCK IN ALASKA, PER KTOO
slides.headline: No version reaches this pole.
slides.body: Flock says it began installing plate readers for a private customer in Alaska the week before October 5th. A crowdsourced map showed eight at two Anchorage Lowe's stores, ADN reports. APD says it doesn't use Flock and has no access to them. Each text governs city agencies.
labels: ILLUSTRATION A READER LIKE THOSE MAPPED AT LOWE'S

slides.headline: October 20th could set the city's clock.
slides.body: The Assembly returns to AO 2026-108 on October 20th, after a work session scheduled for October 14th. The crime center it governs could connect up to 750 cameras. In late August, 238 were registered with APD and 11 integrated, per KTUU.
labels: ONE DISC, ONE CAMERA AUGUST · 238 REGISTERED 11 INTEGRATED
UP TO 750 · A CAPACITY, NOT DRAWN

slides.headline: Where should Anchorage write its number, in code or in policy?

aftercare: Post Tuesday, October 13th, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time, ahead of the October 14th work session. Wednesday or Thursday morning in the same window also works. Don't post after October 20th without updating the deck.
Paste the first comment (sources, the note on the texts, the context invite and the site line) within 60 seconds of posting.

Reply to every comment in the first 60 to 90 minutes. Never write that the September texts allow unlimited retention, that the sponsors dropped the 14 days, or that Lowe's is Flock's customer. The September texts set no day count but require a policy limit, no source says which text moves on October 20th, and Flock hasn't named its customer.

Recheck the Assembly's page at https://www.muni.org/Departments/Assembly/Pages/focus-on-public-safety.aspx before October 14th and again before October 20th. If a new version appears or the action moves again, add a dated comment rather than rewriting the caption.
If a reader says October 20th will regulate the Lowe's cameras, point to slide 07. Each text governs city agencies, and its private camera rules cover only registration and integration with the city.
After 48 hours, note the saves, comments and reposts so the ledger can learn from them.
editor_notes_for_email: This is an UPDATE of No.55 on AO 2026-108, built on the three ordinance texts themselves, which No.55 couldn't reach. The 14-day deletion rule, the warrant and the 2031 end date sit in the August 18th original only. Both September 15th texts are described as containing no 14-day rule and never as unlimited, because the mayor's requires a policy limit. The "articulable operational needs" phrase is quoted from the mayor's (S) only; the S-1 sheet quotes the sponsors' "targeted refinements to the S draft". Flock's customer stays unnamed, the Lowe's count is a crowdsourced map reported by ADN, and October 20th is framed as governing city readers, not store readers. The caption's "S-1 text names no number either" means a retention number; S-1 does carry 30-day and 45-day clocks, which slide 03 shows. ADN's URL path reads 10/06, but the page prints October 7th, so it is cited as 2026-10-07.
